text: Sail from New York to San Francisco the old way, around the bottom of South America, and the trip is about thirteen thousand miles. Cut through Panama, and it is about five thousand two hundred. Before the canal, the long way took about two months. Today, almost no cargo ship sails around Cape Horn at all. So why do ships avoid the bottom of South America? What makes those waters so dangerous? And what happens when the shortcut runs out of water? Let's look at it at its true scale.
Why ships don't sail around South America.

Look at the map. The Americas form one long wall of land, from the Arctic almost all the way to Antarctica. For a ship going between the Atlantic and the Pacific, there were only two natural ways through. A narrow, twisting channel called the Strait of Magellan. Or the open sea further south, past a rock called Cape Horn, into the Drake Passage.

Cape Horn sits on a small island in southern Chile, at about fifty six degrees south. Surprisingly, it is not even the southernmost point of South America. A tiny islet further south holds that title. Two Dutch sailors, Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire, were the first to sail around it, in sixteen sixteen. They named it after Hoorn, a town in the Netherlands. The cape marks the point where the Atlantic meets the Pacific, and it became the most feared corner of the sailing world.

South of the Horn lies the Drake Passage, the gap between South America and Antarctica. At its narrowest, it is about eight hundred kilometres wide, and on average about three thousand four hundred metres deep. Through this gap flows the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the current that circles Antarctica. Estimates put its flow at about one hundred to one hundred and fifty million cubic metres of water every second. The Gulf Stream, measured off Florida, carries about thirty three million. So the Drake Passage funnels several times more water.

Then add the wind. The westerlies blow around the bottom of the planet, and the Andes and the Antarctic Peninsula funnel them into this gap. In winter, gale force winds can blow up to thirty percent of the time. Waves in the Drake Passage often top twelve metres, and west of the Horn, rogue waves can reach up to thirty metres. Near the cape, the sea floor rises, and shallow water makes the waves shorter and steeper. In August, icebergs can drift north of forty degrees south.

Sailors felt every bit of it. In seventeen eighty eight, the British ship Bounty tried to sail west around the Horn. In thirty one days, it made only eighty five miles of headway, then gave up and turned around. Many ships were wrecked here, and many sailors died trying to round the cape.

And still, for centuries, there was no other choice. From the eighteenth to the early twentieth century, fast sailing ships called clippers carried wool, grain and gold from Australia to Europe around Cape Horn. A sailor who survived the trip earned the right to wear a gold earring in his left ear. The last commercial sailing ship to round the Horn with cargo was the Pamir, carrying grain from Australia to England, in nineteen forty nine.

What about the other way through, the Strait of Magellan? It was found by Ferdinand Magellan in fifteen twenty, and it took his ships thirty eight days to get through. The strait is about five hundred and seventy kilometres long, and at its narrowest point it is only about two kilometres wide. It twists between many islands, with narrows and unpredictable winds and currents. Sailing ships often preferred the open, stormy Drake Passage, simply because it gave them room to move. Today, ships in the strait must take a local pilot on board. Its main port, Punta Arenas, was founded in eighteen forty eight and grew as a coal stop for steamships.

The real answer to the whole problem was to cut a new path. Panama is where the Americas are at their thinnest. The French began digging in eighteen eighty one. The United States took over the project in nineteen oh four. Britannica estimates that about twenty five thousand six hundred workers died building the canal, many of them from malaria and yellow fever. On the fifteenth of August, nineteen fourteen, the ship Ancon made the first official crossing.

The Panama Canal is about eighty two kilometres long, from deep water to deep water. But it does not run at sea level. Ships climb over the country. On the Atlantic side, three steps of locks at Gatun lift them twenty six metres up, to a huge artificial lake. On the Pacific side, they come back down through Pedro Miguel and the two steps at Miraflores. The water that does the lifting is fresh rain water from the lake. The older locks use about one hundred and ninety seven million litres for each ship that passes. The crossing itself takes about eight to ten hours.

Now compare the routes. New York to San Francisco, around South America: about thirteen thousand miles, or roughly twenty one thousand kilometres. Through Panama: about five thousand two hundred miles, roughly eight thousand four hundred kilometres. That is less than half. Britannica notes that the old trip took sailing ships about two months. Through the canal, the passage across Panama takes about a day, waiting time included.

Ships kept getting bigger, so in twenty sixteen, Panama opened a third, larger set of locks. Today they take ships up to about three hundred and seventy metres long and fifty one metres wide, with a draft of up to fifteen metres. In twenty twenty one, the canal said almost ninety seven percent of the world's container ships could now fit. A ship the size of the CMA CGM Theodore Roosevelt, almost three hundred and sixty six metres long, rated for nearly fifteen thousand twenty foot containers, can now climb over Panama.

But the shortcut has a weak spot: rain. In twenty twenty three, a severe drought hit Panama, and the lake that feeds the locks dropped. Normally about thirty six ships a day cross. The canal cut that to twenty two, and planned to go as low as eighteen. Some ships waited up to three weeks. A few paid a million dollars or more for a single slot at auction. In October, only five American grain ships bound for Asia crossed, compared with thirty four a year earlier. Others went the long way, through Suez or around Africa. Analysts at McKinsey estimated that around a thousand crossings a year could switch to the Strait of Magellan if limits lasted.

This year, the water came back. In the year to September twenty twenty six, the canal handled thirteen thousand nine hundred and fifty one transits, up about four percent. Canal tonnage reached five hundred and twenty one million tons, a new record. And on the ninth of November, the canal raised its daily slots to thirty four and restored the full fifteen metre draft for its biggest locks. Estimates of its share of world sea trade range from about two and a half to five percent.

So who still sails around Cape Horn? There are no regular cargo routes around it today. A number of cruise ships round it on purpose. Ocean racers in events like the Vendee Globe treat it as the ultimate test. And the bottom of South America is still the backup route, for ships too big for Panama, or for the next time the rain fails.

So, ships avoid the bottom of South America because of the current, the wind, the waves, the ice, and an eighty two kilometre shortcut that saves about half the trip. Here's my question. Would you sail around Cape Horn to earn the gold earring, or take the ten hour shortcut through Panama? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to True Scale for more of the world at its true scale.
